doc.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Losses, politics and the country's culture
title: Using women musicians: Patti Bown, Melba Liston and Clora Bryant
summary: Baker credits Jones with using women in high-profile roles early. Jones says he only asks whether they can play, recalls Clora Bryant at twelve, and Baker mentions Melba Liston's arrangement of Reverie.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Let me ask you something else, because another area that people don’t talk about, where you were taking chances before anybody else was doing that – I’m thinking now of Patti Bown. I’m thinking of Melba.
I’m thinking that you were using women in high-profile positions ten years before it became fashionable to do so.

I never even thought twice about it. Can she play? That’s all I care. Can she play? Clora Bryant I met when I was 12 years old. She was with Sweethearts of Rhythm. You know Clora? Trumpet player. 12 years old. Please. Can she play? That’s all. Whatever it is. I don’t care.

It opened the door for Diva and so many of these other things. When I talk to Ellen Seeling and those people, they tell me, the first time they saw it was when they saw the Quincy Jones band and they saw Melba writing – what is it? Reverie. That she had done the arrangement on.
And all of a sudden they said, look, we don’t have to have an all-girl band unless we want to. We can play in any band.
Unfortunately that has not be replicated by other bands.
